opus-5.5.text:
I think the thing I find most meaningful is that we get to do the work in the open. At Ai2, the goal isn't just to release model weights. It's to release everything: the training data, the code, the intermediate checkpoints, the recipes for post-training, the evaluation setups. That's what we've tried to do with projects like OLMo and Tülu. When you do that, you're not just shipping a product. You're giving the whole research community, academics, startups, people in other countries who don't have hundreds of millions of dollars for compute, a real foundation they can study and build on.

A lot of the frontier labs have gone pretty closed, and I understand the commercial reasons for that. But it means much of the knowledge about how these systems actually get made, especially things like RLHF and post-training, ends up locked inside a handful of companies. I care a lot about keeping a strong open ecosystem, partly for scientific reasons, since you can't really do good science on something you can't inspect, and partly for policy reasons. If we want sensible conversations about AI safety and regulation, people need to understand how these models really work, not just take a company's word for it.

On a more personal level, it's a small, mission-driven place where I can still be pretty hands-on. I get to write, train models, and talk publicly about what we're learning without much friction. That combination, doing real technical work while also explaining it to a broader audience, is something I'd find hard to get almost anywhere else. When someone tells me they reproduced one of our results, or used our data to train their own model for a language or domain we never thought about, that's the moment where it feels worth it.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The thing that keeps me at Ai2 is pretty simple: we're one of the few places that actually releases everything. When we put out a model like OLMo or Tülu, it's not just the weights. It's the data, the training code, the intermediate checkpoints, the evaluation setup, the mistakes we made along the way. That completeness is rare now, and I think it matters more every year as the frontier labs get more closed.

What's meaningful to me personally is that the work compounds for other people. A grad student at a university with four GPUs can take our post-training recipe, understand why each stage is there, and build on it instead of guessing what happened inside a black box. I get emails from people who used our data mixes or our RLHF code, and that feedback loop is a big part of why I do this. It feels like we're keeping the scientific side of the field alive at a moment when a lot of knowledge is going behind closed doors.

There's also a freedom in being a nonprofit. We don't have to pretend a model is better than it is to hit a product launch. If something didn't work, we can just say so in the paper. That honesty is hard to find, and it makes the day-to-day research a lot more enjoyable. I'd rather be in the room where we're trying to explain how these systems actually get made than in the room where the explanation is a marketing deck.
